title: Versola
description: Whole-system health: auth, central and edge on one page. Read the Overview matrix first; open a service's rows only for the part that is not green.

panels.title: Requests/s
panels.description: Requests the ingress controller answers for this environment's Ingress objects, any status.

panels.title: Server errors
panels.description: Share of requests answered 5xx at the front door: the services failing or unreachable (502/503/504). Yellow from 0.1%, red from 1%.

panels.title: Latency ${tail:text}
panels.description: Whole request as the ingress sees it, from the first byte of the request to the last byte of the response, at the quantile chosen in Tail quantile. Includes slow clients.

panels.title: Upstream latency ${tail:text}
panels.description: Time the service behind the ingress took to answer, at the chosen quantile. The gap to the request latency is the network and the client.

panels.title: Pods up
panels.description: Replicas Prometheus can scrape right now. Fewer than expected means a crashed, restarting or unschedulable pod.

panels.title: Requests/s
panels.description: All HTTP requests this service answers, any status.

panels.title: Server errors
panels.description: Share of requests answered 5xx -- the service failing, not the caller erring. Yellow from 0.1%, red from 1%.

panels.title: Latency ${tail:text}
panels.description: Tail latency over every endpoint of the service, at the quantile chosen in the Tail quantile selector at the top (p99 by default: 99 of 100 requests are faster).

panels.title: Refreshes/s
panels.description: Clients exchanging a refresh token for a new access token -- how many sessions are being kept alive.

panels.title: Refresh rejected
panels.description: Share of refresh attempts that were turned down: token expired, revoked, already used, or server error. Users behind these are signed out.

targets.expr: (sum(rate(http_server_requests_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth", route=~"/token.grant_type=refresh_token", status_class!="2xx"}[$__rate_interval])) or vector(0)) / clamp_min(sum(rate(http_server_requests_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth", route=~"/token.grant_type=refresh_token"}[$__rate_interval])), 0.001)

panels.title: DB pool
panels.description: Share of database connections checked out. Near 100% requests start queueing for a connection. Empty if `postgres.pool-metrics-interval` is not set for this service.

panels.title: Heap
panels.description: JVM heap used / heap limit on the fullest pod. Sustained near 100% means GC thrashing, then OOM.

panels.description: Share of requests answered 5xx -- the service failing, not the caller erring. Yellow from 0.1%, red from 1%.

panels.title: Latency ${tail:text}

panels.description: What edge itself adds to a proxied request before it reaches the resource (token and DPoP checks, revocation, permissions, rules), at the quantile chosen in the Tail quantile selector. Proxied traffic is in the graphs below.

panels.title: Proxied/s
panels.description: Requests edge forwards to protected resources -- the traffic edge exists to carry.

panels.title: DB pool
panels.description: Share of database connections checked out. Near 100% requests start queueing for a connection. Empty if `postgres.pool-metrics-interval` is not set for this service.

panels.title: Heap
panels.description: JVM heap used / heap limit on the fullest pod. Sustained near 100% means GC thrashing, then OOM.

panels.title: Requests / s by endpoint
panels.description: Where the traffic goes. `/token?grant_type=…` is split by grant type.

panels.title: Server errors (5xx) / s by endpoint
panels.description: Empty is healthy. Every series here is a bug or an outage of a dependency; the endpoint says where to start.

panels.title: Latency
panels.description: Typical (p50), slow (p95) and slow-tail (p99, and the tail quantiles up to the selected one) request. p99.99 needs roughly 10 000 requests in the rate window to mean anything and p99.999 roughly 100 000; both are rounded up to the histogram bucket edge. Watch the tail -- averages hide the users who are suffering.

panels.title: Slowest endpoints (${tail:text})
panels.description: The five endpoints with the highest p99. If overall latency rose, this says which endpoint to blame.

targets.expr: topk(5, histogram_quantile($tail, sum by (le, method, route) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth"}[$__rate_interval]))))

panels.title: Client errors (4xx) / s by endpoint
panels.description: Callers sending bad or unauthorized requests. Not an outage, but a sudden jump is a broken client, an expired credential or probing.

targets.expr: sum by (method, route, status) (rate(http_server_requests_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth", status_class="4xx"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Requests being served right now
panels.description: In-flight requests per pod. A pod whose line keeps climbing is stuck on something slow; a flat uneven split means poor load balancing.

panels.title: Refreshes / s by result
panels.description: 2xx = new tokens issued. 4xx = refresh refused (expired, revoked, or a refresh token replayed -- compare with revocations on the right). 5xx = our failure.

panels.title: Refresh latency
panels.description: Time to answer a refresh. The dashed line is the 120 ms target for /token.

panels.title: Refresh rejections / s by status
panels.description: Why refreshes fail, by HTTP status. 400/401 are the token being refused; 5xx is the service.

panels.title: Refresh tokens revoked / s
panels.description: Clients and users explicitly revoking a refresh token (logout, 'sign out everywhere'). A spike is followed by rejected refreshes.

panels.title: Token requests / s by grant type
panels.description: authorization_code = a fresh sign-in finishing, refresh_token = an existing session renewing, client_credentials = service-to-service. A healthy system is dominated by refreshes.

panels.title: Token issuance latency ${tail:text} by grant type
panels.description: p99 of each token grant. The dashed line is the 120 ms /token target.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile($tail, sum by (le, route) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth", route=~"/token.*"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: Authorize requests / s by outcome
panels.description: silent = the user already had a session and went straight through; interactive = the user must sign in; error = the request was rejected (reasons on the right).

panels.title: Authorize errors / s by reason
panels.description: Why /authorize refused. Mostly integration mistakes in a client application (bad redirect URI, missing PKCE, …).

panels.title: Sign-ins started vs completed
panels.description: Users who began signing in vs users who finished. The gap is abandonment and failure -- the conversion of the funnel.

panels.title: Sign-in completion rate
panels.description: Share of started sign-ins that completed. A drop with no traffic change means users are getting stuck -- check the step failures next.

panels.title: Failed attempts by step
panels.description: For each sign-in step (password, OTP, passkey, …), the share of attempts that failed. Points at the factor users trip over.

targets.expr: sum by (step) (rate(auth_conversation_step_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth", result="failed"}[$__rate_interval])) / clamp_min(sum by (step) (rate(auth_conversation_step_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth"}[$__rate_interval])), 0.001)

panels.title: Hashes waiting for a permit
panels.description: Hashes queued behind the admission semaphore. Non-zero means logins arrive faster than this pod admits them (`argon2.max-concurrent`): add replicas or permits.

panels.title: Permits in use
panels.description: Hashes being computed over the permits the pod has. At 100% CPU no longer follows demand and the queue on the left starts to grow.

targets.expr: sum by (pod) (argon2_hashes_in_flight{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth"}) / clamp_min(max by (pod) (argon2_max_concurrent{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth"}), 1)

panels.title: Hash wait and hash time (${tail:text})
panels.description: The wait is the part of a login's latency that more replicas remove; the hash itself is the cost of the parameters.

panels.title: Hashes / s
panels.description: Password hashes and verifications completed.

panels.title: Refused by a rate limit / s
panels.description: Calls answered 429, by policy. Only `enforce` policies appear here. A policy that refuses a steady share of one client's traffic is working; one that refuses many clients at once is too tight (see the share below).

panels.title: Would be refused / s (shadow)
panels.description: What a `shadow` policy counted and did not refuse. This is the number to read before switching a policy to enforce: if it is zero over a normal week the limit is safe, if it is not, ask who it would have refused (the log line per policy, once a minute) before enforcing.

panels.title: Share of calls a policy refuses
panels.description: Refused (or would be) / all calls the policy decided, shadow included. Above 1% sustained, the policy is cutting into normal traffic: raise its limit or burst, or narrow what it is keyed on, before it enforces.

panels.title: Keys tracked per policy
panels.description: Distinct callers (clients, users, addresses) a policy holds a bucket for, on the fullest pod. Dashed line: the 100,000 cap per policy, past which new keys share one overflow bucket.

panels.title: Keys over the cap / s
panels.description: Calls counted in the shared overflow bucket because the policy was at its key cap. Empty is healthy; non-zero is either far more callers than the cap or an attacker sending distinct keys, and those callers share one limit.

panels.title: Requests in flight against the limit
panels.description: Requests this pod is serving, the busiest second, and the most it admits at once (the adaptive limit when adaptive is on). Peak near the limit means the pod is close to refusing; a limit that falls while in flight does not is the pod slowing down. Empty while the overload policy is off.

panels.title: Refused by overload protection / s
panels.description: Requests turned away because the pod was full. `mode` enforce answered 503 with Retry-After; shadow served the request and only counted it, so the number is what enforcing would have refused. Tiers: `start` (new sign-ins) go first, `continuation` next, `critical` last. Sustained shadow refusals: raise the limit or add pods before enforcing; any enforce refusals: the pod is saturated now.

panels.title: Adaptive limit — share of its ceiling
panels.description: How much of `maxLimit` the adaptive limit currently allows. Near 100% the pod keeps up; low means round-trip times grew and the limit backed off to protect it. Stays flat when adaptive is off.

panels.title: Round trip by tier and event-loop lag
panels.description: What the adaptive limit follows: the mean time to answer per tier, and how late a 10 ms timer fires (a stalled pod completes no calls, so only lateness shows it). Lag of hundreds of milliseconds is a pod that is not scheduling work: GC, CPU throttling or a blocked thread, not a lack of capacity.

panels.title: Calls to other services — latency ${tail:text}
panels.description: How long this service waits for each service it calls. Part of our own latency.

panels.title: Calls to other services — in flight
panels.description: Outbound requests in flight per target, including those queued for a pooled connection (the outbound pool). Where the pool is too small this climbs long before CPU or latency averages move; a line pinned at the pool size is the outbound pool being the limit.

panels.title: Calls to other services — failures / s
panels.description: Calls that failed: connection errors or a 5xx from the other side. Empty is healthy.

panels.title: Outbound guard — in flight against the limit
panels.description: Calls the guard has let through per peer, and the most it allows at once. In flight pinned at the limit means the peer is where this service waits: read the queue and the refusals next. Empty until the outbound guard is on for this service.

panels.title: Outbound guard — queued calls and wait ${tail:text}
panels.description: Calls waiting for a place to a peer, and how long they waited (seconds, at the selected quantile). A queue that keeps growing is a peer slower than the traffic sent to it; the wait is time added to every call behind it.

panels.title: Outbound guard — refused / s
panels.description: Calls the guard refused: `queue_full`, `queue_timeout`, `circuit_open`, `request_timeout`. `mode` shadow means the call was still made and only counted: what enforcing would refuse. Read shadow for a week before switching a peer to enforce.

panels.title: Outbound guard — circuit breaker
panels.description: Per peer: 0 closed (calls pass), 1 half-open (probing), 2 open (calls are refused without being made). Open means the peer is failing more than the policy tolerates; it reopens by itself after the open time.

panels.title: Outbound guard — retries denied / s
panels.description: Retries the retry budget refused, so a failing peer is not hit with a second wave. Non-zero is the budget working; sustained means the peer is failing most calls.

panels.title: Configuration served from the snapshot — age
panels.description: Age of the configuration a cache is serving from its database snapshot because central could not be reached at startup. Zero is live. Anything else means that pod runs on configuration central last confirmed that long ago, and keeps retrying central in the background.

panels.title: CPU cores in use
panels.description: Per pod. Uneven lines mean uneven load balancing or a hot pod. Compare with the pod's CPU limit.

panels.title: CPU throttled
panels.description: Share of scheduler periods in which the pod hit its CPU limit and was paused. Any sustained value adds latency that no CPU graph explains. Empty when the pod has no CPU limit.

targets.expr: sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{namespace="$namespace", container="auth"}[$__rate_interval])) / clamp_min(sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{namespace="$namespace", container="auth"}[$__rate_interval])), 0.001)

panels.title: Time in garbage collection
panels.description: Share of wall-clock time the JVM is paused for GC. Above a few percent the service is starved of memory.

panels.title: DB pool in use
panels.description: Checked-out connections / pool size, per pod. The pool is sampled; a short saturation can pass between samples, so also read the wait panel on the Database board. Empty if `postgres.pool-metrics-interval` is not set for this service.

targets.expr: sum by (pod) (db_client_connection_count{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth", state="used"}) / clamp_min(sum by (pod) (db_client_connection_max{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="auth"}), 1)

panels.title: Heap
panels.description: Heap in use against its limit. A sawtooth is normal (GC working); a floor that keeps rising is a leak.

panels.title: Threads
panels.description: Live JVM threads per pod. Unbounded growth is a thread leak.

panels.title: Config changes by result

panels.title: Requests / s by resource
panels.description: The same traffic grouped by protected resource (fapi-core, fapi-pay, central, …) -- which API is being used.

panels.title: Where a proxied request spends its time (mean)
panels.description: Average time per proxied request, split into the resource's own answer, the token lookup at auth, and what edge adds on top. The three add up to the proxy latency.

targets.expr: sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_sum{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", route=~"/resources/.*"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", route=~"/resources/.*"}[$__rate_interval])) - sum(rate(http_client_request_duration_seconds_sum{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", peer!~"versola-(auth|central)[:.].*"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", route=~"/resources/.*"}[$__rate_interval])) - sum(rate(http_client_request_duration_seconds_sum{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", peer=~"versola-auth[:.].*", route="userinfo"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", route=~"/resources/.*"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Edge overhead (measured)
panels.description: Time edge itself spends on a request before it reaches the resource: token and DPoP checks, revocation, permissions, rules. Requests that waited on auth (a /userinfo call, a refresh of an expired token) are left out and shown on the next graph. The wait for the resource is not included. Measured per request in edge (edge_proxy_overhead_seconds), so the quantiles here are real. Dashed line: 15 ms budget. Empty until edge runs a build that includes the metric.

panels.title: Edge overhead by what it waited on (${tail:text})
panels.description: The same overhead split by whether the request waited on auth: none (edge's own work), userinfo (the /userinfo call an endpoint asks for), refresh (an expired token refreshed at auth). The last two are mostly auth's latency, so a high line there is read as auth being slow, not edge. No label on an edge build before it was added.

panels.title: Requests being served right now
panels.description: In-flight requests per pod. A pod whose line keeps climbing is stuck on something slow; a flat uneven split means poor load balancing.

panels.title: Revoked tokens held in cache
panels.description: Entries in the revocation list edge checks every token against.

panels.title: Revocation sync lag
panels.description: Per pod. Flat at 0 is healthy: the last refresh succeeded. It is only written when a refresh happens, so a non-zero value means refreshes are failing and shows how long the pod has been without one.

panels.title: Revocation list refresh failures / s
panels.description: Any failure means revocations are not reaching edge, and revoked tokens may still be accepted.

panels.title: Replay protection (DPoP) pressure
panels.description: How often the in-memory replay-proof store overflowed. Empty is healthy; sustained values mean it is undersized for the traffic.

panels.title: Refused by a rate limit / s
panels.description: Calls answered 429, by policy. Only `enforce` policies appear here. A policy that refuses a steady share of one client's traffic is working; one that refuses many clients at once is too tight (see the share below).

panels.title: Would be refused / s (shadow)
panels.description: What a `shadow` policy counted and did not refuse. This is the number to read before switching a policy to enforce: if it is zero over a normal week the limit is safe, if it is not, ask who it would have refused (the log line per policy, once a minute) before enforcing.

panels.title: Share of calls a policy refuses
panels.description: Refused (or would be) / all calls the policy decided, shadow included. Above 1% sustained, the policy is cutting into normal traffic: raise its limit or burst, or narrow what it is keyed on, before it enforces.

panels.title: Keys tracked per policy
panels.description: Distinct callers (clients, users, addresses) a policy holds a bucket for, on the fullest pod. Dashed line: the 100,000 cap per policy, past which new keys share one overflow bucket.

panels.title: Keys over the cap / s
panels.description: Calls counted in the shared overflow bucket because the policy was at its key cap. Empty is healthy; non-zero is either far more callers than the cap or an attacker sending distinct keys, and those callers share one limit.

panels.title: Pods the limit is divided by
panels.description: `in force` is the number each pod divides a limit by, and where it came from: `dns` (replicas-from) or `policy` (the replicas of the policy set). `pods serving traffic` is how many pods answer. When they differ the limit is wrong by that factor: with more pods than in force the edge allows too much, with fewer it refuses too early.

panels.title: Where the caller's address comes from
panels.description: `forwarded`: read from the proxy's header. `socket`: the connection's peer, right when callers reach the edge directly; behind a proxy or load balancer it is the proxy's own address, the same for everyone, so address limits count everyone together. `forwarded_missing`: client-ip is forwarded but the header was absent or not an address: a misconfiguration, or a caller bypassing the proxy.

panels.title: Requests in flight against the limit
panels.description: Requests this pod is serving, the busiest second, and the most it admits at once (the adaptive limit when adaptive is on). Peak near the limit means the pod is close to refusing; a limit that falls while in flight does not is the pod slowing down. Empty while the overload policy is off.

panels.title: Refused by overload protection / s
panels.description: Requests turned away because the pod was full. `mode` enforce answered 503 with Retry-After; shadow served the request and only counted it, so the number is what enforcing would have refused. Tiers: `start` (new sign-ins) go first, `continuation` next, `critical` last. Sustained shadow refusals: raise the limit or add pods before enforcing; any enforce refusals: the pod is saturated now.

panels.title: Adaptive limit — share of its ceiling
panels.description: How much of `maxLimit` the adaptive limit currently allows. Near 100% the pod keeps up; low means round-trip times grew and the limit backed off to protect it. Stays flat when adaptive is off.

panels.title: Round trip by tier and event-loop lag
panels.description: What the adaptive limit follows: the mean time to answer per tier, and how late a 10 ms timer fires (a stalled pod completes no calls, so only lateness shows it). Lag of hundreds of milliseconds is a pod that is not scheduling work: GC, CPU throttling or a blocked thread, not a lack of capacity.

panels.title: Calls to other services — latency ${tail:text}
panels.description: How long this service waits for each service it calls. Part of our own latency.

panels.title: Calls to other services — in flight
panels.description: Outbound requests in flight per target, including those queued for a pooled connection (the outbound pool). Where the pool is too small this climbs long before CPU or latency averages move; a line pinned at the pool size is the outbound pool being the limit.

panels.title: Calls to other services — failures / s
panels.description: Calls that failed: connection errors or a 5xx from the other side. Empty is healthy.

panels.title: Outbound guard — in flight against the limit
panels.description: Calls the guard has let through per peer, and the most it allows at once. In flight pinned at the limit means the peer is where this service waits: read the queue and the refusals next. Empty until the outbound guard is on for this service.

panels.title: Outbound guard — queued calls and wait ${tail:text}
panels.description: Calls waiting for a place to a peer, and how long they waited (seconds, at the selected quantile). A queue that keeps growing is a peer slower than the traffic sent to it; the wait is time added to every call behind it.

panels.title: Outbound guard — refused / s
panels.description: Calls the guard refused: `queue_full`, `queue_timeout`, `circuit_open`, `request_timeout`. `mode` shadow means the call was still made and only counted: what enforcing would refuse. Read shadow for a week before switching a peer to enforce.

panels.title: Outbound guard — circuit breaker
panels.description: Per peer: 0 closed (calls pass), 1 half-open (probing), 2 open (calls are refused without being made). Open means the peer is failing more than the policy tolerates; it reopens by itself after the open time.

panels.title: Outbound guard — retries denied / s
panels.description: Retries the retry budget refused, so a failing peer is not hit with a second wave. Non-zero is the budget working; sustained means the peer is failing most calls.

panels.title: Configuration served from the snapshot — age
panels.description: Age of the configuration a cache is serving from its database snapshot because central could not be reached at startup. Zero is live. Anything else means that pod runs on configuration central last confirmed that long ago, and keeps retrying central in the background.

panels.title: CPU cores in use
panels.description: Per pod. Uneven lines mean uneven load balancing or a hot pod. Compare with the pod's CPU limit.

panels.title: CPU throttled
panels.description: Share of scheduler periods in which the pod hit its CPU limit and was paused. Any sustained value adds latency that no CPU graph explains. Empty when the pod has no CPU limit.

targets.expr: sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{namespace="$namespace", container="edge"}[$__rate_interval])) / clamp_min(sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{namespace="$namespace", container="edge"}[$__rate_interval])), 0.001)

panels.title: Time in garbage collection
panels.description: Share of wall-clock time the JVM is paused for GC. Above a few percent the service is starved of memory.

panels.title: DB pool in use
panels.description: Checked-out connections / pool size, per pod. The pool is sampled; a short saturation can pass between samples, so also read the wait panel on the Database board. Empty if `postgres.pool-metrics-interval` is not set for this service.

targets.expr: sum by (pod) (db_client_connection_count{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge", state="used"}) / clamp_min(sum by (pod) (db_client_connection_max{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="edge"}), 1)

panels.title: Heap
panels.description: Heap in use against its limit. A sawtooth is normal (GC working); a floor that keeps rising is a leak.

panels.title: Threads
panels.description: Live JVM threads per pod. Unbounded growth is a thread leak.
